t: Valid Subarrays With Exactly One Peak
o: A peak is a strictly local maximum at an interior index. A valid subarray must contain exactly one peak i, start within k steps left of it, and end within k steps right of it. In Example 1 (peak at 1, k=1): left choices {0,1} and right choices {1,2} give 2*2 = 4 subarrays. Example 3 (peak at 2, k=2): 3 left choices * 2 right choices = 6. Example 2 has no peaks, so 0. Since left and right extents are independent once the peak is fixed, each peak contributes a simple product; summing over peaks is O(n).
k: For a peak at i, the left endpoint can be any of max(0, i-k)..i and the right endpoint any of i..min(n-1, i+k).
Each peak contributes (i - max(0,i-k) + 1) * (min(n-1,i+k) - i + 1) subarrays; sum over all peaks.

a.i: Fix a peak i. Containing i forces l <= i <= r; the distance constraints bound l >= i-k and r <= i+k, and array bounds clip further. The choices multiply because they are independent, giving the closed-form product per peak.
s: If nums[i] > nums[i-1] and nums[i] > nums[i+1], it is a peak.
Add (i - max(0, i-k) + 1) * (min(n-1, i+k) - i + 1) to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) work per index.

a.n: Approach 2: Enumerate endpoints around each peak
a.i: Equivalently, for each peak, loop over all valid l and r pairs and count them. This is the literal translation of the definition and is useful for verifying the product formula on small inputs.
s: For each peak i, for l from max(0, i-k) to i, for r from i to min(n-1, i+k): increment a counter.
a.t: O(n·k^2) worst case — nested loops over endpoint ranges per peak.

w: Give the product formula directly; the nested-loop version is only a sanity check. Watch for overflow: the count can reach roughly n·k^2 scale, so use 64-bit accumulation in C++/Java. Edge cases: n = 1 or 2 (no interior peaks, answer 0), plateaus (equal neighbors are not peaks), k >= n (clipped by array bounds). Follow-up: count subarrays with at least one peak, or with peaks in a value range.
